Discussion 4.1. Position of pretraining for OOD generalization With the rapid development of pretrained models, includ- ing large language models like ChatGPT and LLaMA [72], and large multi-modal models like GPT-4V [58] and LLaV A [48], nowadays typically we tend to take advan- tage of pretraining in real applications. Despite their re- markable performance, current studies show that they are far from perfect and still suffer from performance degrada- tion under distribution shifts, even for GPT-3.5 [81, 85] and GPT-4V [93]. Besides, it is hard to collect sufficient diverse data to train or fine-tune large models due to high expenses and privacy issues in some areas like medical care, where distribution shifts prevail. Thus the problem of OOD gen- eralization still holds great significance in the era of large pretrained models. However, with the existence of pretrained models, proper evaluation of OOD generalization becomes a natural prob- lem [83]. Since we focus on the ability of models generaliz- ing from training data to test data, strong pretrained weights naturally bring about possible test information leakage as we have analyzed in Sec. 2.1. Kumar et al. [37] also provide theoretical analyses that with good pretrained weights and a strong distribution shift, LP will outperform FT in that FT can distort the pretrained features, which are already good enough to generalize to test data. Our work serves as an ini- tial effort to provide a better evaluation protocol for OOD generalization under pretraining. Recently, there have been works showing that pretraining on larger datasets with larger architecture backbones greatly improves test performance in OOD tasks [31, 77, 84], and some directly design algorithms for better utilization of pretrained weights to improve test domain performance [47, 62]. We believe this is an interesting and meaning- ful research direction of valuable practical usage. If we di- rectly focus on improving test performance, we should em- ploy pretrained weights that are as strong and powerful as possible. However, for a fairer and more accurate evaluation of OOD generalization from training data to test data dur- ing the fine-tuning stage, we should seek pretrained weights that exhibit less test data information leakage. 4.2. OOD model selection Model selection is another important topic for OOD gen- eralization. DomainBed [19] has pointed out that oracle model selection (test-domain validation) leaks test data in- formation in domain generalization. A similar problem also exists in subpopulation shift and is even more severe. Idrissi et al. [28] demonstrate that model selection based on the av- erage accuracy on an IID validation set can lead to signif- icant performance degradation compared with using worst group accuracy. The latter strategy utilizes the group label information, which should be considered as oracle model selection at least for methods claiming no need for group information. In this paper, we adhere to DomainBed’s IID validation (training-domain validation) to prevent test in- formation leakage for the guarantee of a fair and accurate comparison, but it does not mean that IID validation is the only right way for model selection. Considering the natu- ral inconsistency of performance on IID validation data and test data [70], maybe IID validation is not the best approach to guiding model selection. Improving the model selection strategy remains a fundamental research problem for OOD generalization in the future. 4.3. Datasets for domain generalization It has been a long time since domain generalization algo- rithms are primarily evaluated on relatively small datasets, e.g. Colored MNIST [1], Rotated MNIST [18], PACS [39], VLCS [30], OfficeHome [74], and TerraInc [3]. Based on our analyses in this paper, our recommendation for expand- ing the number of test domains requires the establishment of larger datasets, and it is the same if we want to add more datasets to the leaderboard of training from scratch, which only DomainNet [59] and NICO++ [90] can sup- port currently. It is much more challenging to construct a large, high-quality, and balanced dataset for domain gen- eralization than to construct one for IID generalization, as it involves creating many domains with common classes. Recently, Lynch et al. [54] released a dataset Spawrious for better evaluation of OOD generalization, whose data is completely generated and collected from stable diffusion models. This provides a new direction for constructing do- main generalization datasets with much lower cost. 5. Related Work Given multiple training domains, the task of domain gener- alization focuses on improving the generalization ability of models on unseen test domains. Here we introduce related work of domain generalization from two perspectives: algo- rithms and evaluation. For other Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization algorithms, you may refer to the survey of OOD generalization [66]. For a more detailed review of their evaluation, you may refer to the survey of OOD eval- uation [83]. Algorithms There are many types of domain generaliza- tion algorithms. The most typical practice is learning repre- sentations that are invariant across training domains [42– 45, 55, 61, 79]. Other common types of algorithms in- clude data augmentation [64, 75, 80], meta learning [2, 40, 41, 46], sample reweighting [87], and self-supervised learning [20, 89]. Recently, more works focus on the fun- damental properties and mechanisms of generalization, in- cluding emphasizing hard-to-learn features [25] or sam- ples [26], flatness [7, 91, 92], heterogeneity [49, 53, 71], etc. For a more detailed review of domain generalization algorithms, you may refer to the surveys of domain gener- alization [76, 95]. Evaluation To facilitate the appropriate evaluation of do- main generalization algorithms, there are a number of datasets built with different types of distribution shifts. Among the most widely used ones, PACS [39], Office- Home [74] and DomainNet [59] depict the distribution shift via the change of image styles. VLCS [30] is collected from multiple sources and treats each source as a domain. NICO++ [88, 90] creates different contexts based on var- ious elements like background, object color, season, etc. TerraInc [3] employs the camera view to generate distribu- tion shifts. Apart from these datasets, Gulrajani and Lopez- Paz [19] establishes DomainBed, a benchmark along with a comprehensive evaluation protocol by incorporating hy- perparameter search into the evaluation pipeline, to bring convenience and fairness to the development and compari- son of domain generalization algorithms. B. Additional experiments for the analyses of pretraining Note that for both linear-probing (LP) and fine-tuning (FT), we have searched the best hyperparameters on a validation set that shares the same distribution with the training do- mains, following the original protocol of DomainBed. B.1. LP v.s. FT for supervised pretrained ResNet-50 Results of LP and FT with supervised pretrained ResNet-50 on DomainNet and NICO++ are shown in Tab. 7. We can see that the phenomenon of LP outperforming FT still ex- ists in some domains, which demonstrates the prevalence of such phenomenon under the standard domain generalization protocol. B.2. LP v.s. FT for various pretraining We change different pretraining architectures and methods. For PACS and VLCS, we conduct experiments with the same pretraining strategies and network backbones as in Tab. 3. For TerraInc, DomainNet, NICO++, we conduct experiments only with MoCo-v2 pretrained ResNet-50 and MoCo-v3 pretrained ViT-B/16. As shown in Tab. 6 and Tab. 8, we find that in these datasets, self-supervised pre- training still guarantees that linear-probing does not outper- form fine-tuning, which is beneficial for a fairer comparison between algorithms. C. Detailed Leaderboards Next, we present detailed leaderboards of each dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/h- yu16/DomainBed-v2 . Our code is mostly based on the implementation of DomainBed1. Since most results on TerraInc fluctuate a lot, exhibiting a large standard devia- tion [19], we do not include this dataset in our leaderboards. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: This paper identifies two critical risks of test data information leakage in the current domain generalization (DG) evaluation protocol: the use of supervised pretraining on ImageNet and reliance on oracle model selection. The authors propose significant modifications to the protocol: employing self-supervised pretraining or training models from scratch, and evaluating algorithms across multiple test domains. Through comprehensive experiments, they provide empirical evidence that these changes lead to a more precise and fair evaluation of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization ability. The study reruns ten representative DG algorithms under the revised protocol, introducing new leaderboards that reveal substantial shifts in algorithm rankings, highlighting the improved accuracy of the proposed evaluation. A key finding is that self-supervised pretraining leaderboards correlate more closely with 'training from scratch' leaderboards, underscoring their effectiveness in mitigating test data information leakage.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The methodology involves an empirical analysis of the current DG evaluation protocol and the proposal of two main modifications. For pretraining, the authors compared Linear Probing (LP) and Fine-Tuning (FT) with ImageNet supervised pretrained ResNet-50, observing that LP often matched or surpassed FT performance, suggesting over-reliance on pretrained features. This was further supported by experiments varying frozen layers and Fr 4echet Inception Distance (FID) correlations. To address this, they investigated self-supervised pretraining methods (MoCo, MoCo-v2, SimCLR, SimCLR-v2 for ResNet-50; MoCo-v3 for ViT-B/16) and training from scratch, demonstrating that self-supervised pretraining successfully mitigated the LP vs. FT issue. For oracle model selection, they experimented with DomainNet and NICO++ datasets, varying the number of test domains (K) in the evaluation. They empirically showed that increasing K significantly reduced information leakage stemming from oracle model selection. The modified protocol for new leaderboards involved using MoCo-v2/MoCo-v3 for pretraining, adopting a leave-one-group-out strategy for multi-domain datasets like DomainNet and NICO++ (yielding two test domains), and adjusting hyperparameter search with fewer trials (10 trials for 2 random seeds).
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The research utilized several widely-used domain generalization benchmark datasets: PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, Terra Incognita, DomainNet, and NICO++. Various backbone architectures were employed, including ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and ViT-B/16. Pretraining strategies encompassed standard ImageNet supervised pretraining, as well as several self-supervised methods like MoCo, MoCo-v2, SimCLR, SimCLR-v2 (for ResNet-50), and MoCo-v3 (for ViT-B/16). Additionally, experiments included training models from scratch on sufficiently large datasets (DomainNet and NICO++). Ten representative domain generalization algorithms were re-evaluated: ERM, SWAD, RSC, GroupDRO, Fishr, CORAL, MMD, SagNet, IRM, and Mixup. The evaluation protocol largely followed DomainBed, but with modifications such as a leave-one-group-out strategy for DomainNet and NICO++ to enable evaluation on multiple test domains, and reduced hyperparameter search trials (10 trials for 2 random seeds instead of 20 trials for 3 seeds) to manage computational costs. Training iterations were set at 5,000 for smaller datasets and 10,000-15,000 for larger ones, with 60,000 iterations for training from scratch. The Adam optimizer with a Cosine Annealing Scheduler was consistently used.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The paper acknowledges several limitations within the broader context of domain generalization evaluation. Firstly, the standard IID validation (training-domain validation) used for fair comparison, while necessary to prevent test information leakage, might not be the optimal strategy for guiding model selection in OOD generalization due to the inherent inconsistency between IID validation performance and unseen test data performance. Secondly, the recommendations for using multiple test domains and training from scratch are constrained by the current availability of large, high-quality, and balanced datasets; only DomainNet and NICO++ were found suitable for these extensive evaluations. Lastly, the emphasis on self-supervised pretraining or training from scratch for fair evaluation might create a gap with real-world applications where leveraging the most powerful (often supervised) pretrained models is common practice to achieve maximum performance, suggesting a trade-off between evaluating true OOD generalization ability and maximizing predictive performance in deployment.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Future research directions include exploring the appropriate position of pretraining for OOD generalization, especially with the rapid development of powerful large pretrained models. This involves balancing the objective of purely evaluating a model's generalization ability from training data against the practical goal of maximizing test performance through the strongest available pretraining. Another key direction is to improve OOD model selection strategies, aiming to develop methods that can more effectively guide model selection despite the acknowledged inconsistency between IID validation data and unseen test data. Lastly, the paper highlights the critical need for the development of new, larger-scale domain generalization datasets that can support robust evaluations with multiple test domains and enable training from scratch. This could involve exploring novel dataset construction methods, such as utilizing generative models.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: Unsupervised elimination of visual spurious correlations for OOD-robust image classification.  Current causal or counterfactual methods either 1) assume the nuisance attribute is annotated (Waterbirds, AutoACER), 2) rely on costly human editing (Counterfactually-Augmented Data), or 3) work only at the feature level without touching the raw pixel statistics that give rise to distribution-shift brittleness (IRM, Fourier pruning studies).  A practical, scalable technique that automatically discovers and neutralises spurious cues—textures, backgrounds, co-occurring objects—without any attribute labels is still missing.  Solving this would drastically widen the applicability of causal robustness techniques to real-world, large-scale data where the set of harmful correlations is unknown a-priori.
Methods: We propose AutoCF-Diff: Automatic CounterFactual generation with Diffusion models plus invariance regularisation.  
1. Spurious-cue discovery (unsupervised):
   a. Train a frozen vision-language model (e.g.
      CLIP) to obtain token-level relevance maps (GradCAM/Attention-Rollout) for each training image.
   b. Apply spectral clustering on relevance maps across the dataset; the smallest, most class-invariant cluster is treated as the ‘core object mask’, everything else as potential spurious regions.
2. Counterfactual synthesis:
   a. Use an in-painting diffusion model (StableDiffusion-Inpaint) conditioned on the original text prompt or CLIP embedding to *randomise only the spurious region* while keeping the core mask untouched.  Multiple diverse backgrounds/styles are generated per image.
   b. Conversely, generate object-removed versions (mask out core, in-paint with background) to measure causal effects.
3. Invariance learning objective:
   a. For each original–counterfactual pair (x, x'), impose Causal Consistency Loss  LCC = CE(f(x), y)+CE(f(x'), y)+ λ‖f^l(x)-f^l(x')‖₂  where f^l is a late feature layer.
   b. Add Causal Effect Regularisation (AutoACER) but *estimate effects through these synthetic interventions*, removing need for attribute labels.
4. Spectral robustness augmentation: apply randomized Fourier phase swapping inside the spurious region during diffusion to diversify low-/high-frequency cues.
5. Training loop alternates between (1) refreshing masks with updated classifier gradients and (2) updating classifier + lightweight mask predictor; converges when causal consistency plateaus.
Distinctiveness:  (i) no human or attribute supervision; (ii) operates in pixel space, directly attacking texture/background cues; (iii) unifies generative counterfactuals with causal-effect regularisation.
Experimental Setup: Datasets:  Waterbirds, CelebA (Blond-Male), Spawrious, NICO++ (‘context’ splits), plus ImageNet-9 with synthetic background correlation and standard OOD sets (ImageNet-A/R/C, CIFAR-10-C).
Backbones: ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16.
Baselines: ERM, IRM, GroupDRO, CAD (human-edited), AutoACER (with oracle attribute), Fourier Mix, CLIP zero-shot.
Metrics: 1) Worst-group accuracy (WGA). 2) Average OOD accuracy on held-out contexts. 3) ∆Prob (change in prediction when swapping background). 4) Fourier High-Frequency Fraction (HFF) sensitivity. 5) Robustness under common corruptions (mCE) and OOD natural distribution shifts.
Protocols: follow DomainBed for validation; report mean±std over 3 seeds.  Ablations: (i) mask discovery quality vs. manual masks, (ii) diffusion diversity k, (iii) removing spectral swaps, (iv) replacing diffusion with simple colour jitter to show necessity.
Result: We expect AutoCF-Diff to:
• raise WGA on Waterbirds from ~72% (best prior w/o spurious labels) to >85%, matching methods that use oracle attributes.
• cut ∆Prob by >50% relative to ERM, indicating minimal background reliance.
• lower HFF sensitivity, aligning with effectively-robust models in Fourier lens study.
• improve ImageNet-C mCE by 5-10 points over ERM and outperform CAD despite zero manual edits.
• Ablations confirm both diffusion-based counterfactuals and causal regularisation contribute additively.
Conclusion: AutoCF-Diff offers a label-free pipeline to generate high-fidelity visual counterfactuals and integrate them into a causal-effect learning objective, substantially narrowing the gap between ordinary ERM and oracle-informed robust models.  Academically, it bridges generative diffusion modelling, causal regularisation, and spectral robustness, opening avenues for analysing learned causal masks and for extending to video/action recognition.  Practically, it scales to web-scale data where spurious cues are unknown, providing a drop-in training module for industry-grade classifiers.  Future work: adaptive diffusion guidance for concept shift, integration with adversarial training for joint adversarial-OOD robustness, and releasing an open-source counterfactual-image benchmark generated by this method.
